newsitem.title: USA: Insider says Abrego led Mexican drugs cartel.
newsitem.headline: Insider says Abrego led Mexican drugs cartel.

text.p: A man who helped the notorious Gulf drug cartel in northern Mexico ship thousands of tons of cocaine into the United States said on Tuesday that Juan Garcia Abrego, once on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list, was the head of the organisation.
Jaime Rivas Gonzalez told a jury that he had been told by top members of the cartel that Garcia Abrego was "El Senor" -- The Man -- whom all obeyed.

"He asked me if I knew El Senor (The Man) and I said 'what man?' He answered 'Juan Garcia Abrego,'" Rivas testified about a conversation with a cartel lieutenant nicknamed El Profe (short for The Professor).

Rivas also said he saw Garcia Abrego and Luis Garcia Medrano, the alleged second-in-command of the Gulf Cartel, together at a horse race in Mexico in 1989, and was later told by Medrano that Garcia Abrego was El Patron, the leader of the organisation.
Garcia Abrego, captured in Monterrey, Mexico in January and flown to Houston for trial, is being tried on 22 drug and money-laundering counts and faces life in prison if convicted.
His attorneys say prosecutors have the wrong man and have implied that Medrano, considered by prosecutors to be the number-two man in the organisation, actually headed the cartel.
Rivas testified on Tuesday that Medrano, captured last year by Mexican authorities, recently died in a jail in Mexico, which was confirmed by defence attorney Tony Canales and other officials.

A representative of the Mexican Attorney General's office told reporters that Medrano died in August of liver problems brought on by diabetes. He said the United States tried twice to extradite Medrano to testify in the Garcia Abrego trial, but the requests were denied by the Mexican government.

Rivas said he drove huge shipments of cocaine for the cartel from the Rio Grande Valley in South Texas to Houston and other cities, for which he was paid $400 a kilogram. He said he became a millionaire before being caught. He is serving a 10-year jail sentence.
Under questioning from defence attorneys, Rivas said he originally was sentenced to life in prison, but the punishment was reduced in exchange for his testimony in seven separate drug trials.
Rivas also said that cartel members bribed Mexican and U.S. border officials in exchange for them turning a blind eye to trucks full of cocaine at checkpoints at and near the U.S.-Mexico border.

Prosecutors allege the Gulf Cartel served as the shipping arm of Colombia's Cali cartel, flying tons of cocaine into airstrips in the Mexican state of Tabasco. From there, the Gulf Cartel flew the cocaine to airstrips in Tamaulipas and ferried the drugs across the U.S.-Mexico border in airplanes, trucks and on the backs of human mules.
